questions.q: What is the key idea behind "risk budgeting" as opposed to simply allocating equal capital to each position?
options: Risk budgeting means every position must have exactly equal dollar value
Risk budgeting means deliberately deciding how much of the portfolio's total risk each position should carry, since equal dollar amounts rarely mean equal risk once volatility and correlation differ
Risk budgeting only applies to fixed income portfolios
Risk budgeting is identical to leverage
questions.explain: Two positions of equal dollar size can contribute very different amounts of risk depending on their volatility and correlation with the rest of the portfolio. Risk budgeting sizes positions to hit an intended risk allocation, not just an equal dollar split.

questions.q: How is a position's risk contribution to total portfolio volatility computed?
options: By multiplying the position's weight by its marginal contribution to portfolio volatility (derived from the covariance matrix)
By dividing the position's dollar value by total equity
By counting the number of shares held
By looking only at the position's own standalone volatility, ignoring correlations
questions.explain: Risk contribution for position i is w_i times its marginal contribution to risk, where the marginal contribution comes from the covariance matrix — this properly accounts for how that position's risk interacts with the rest of the portfolio, not just its own volatility in isolation.

questions.q: What does leverage do to a strategy's Sharpe ratio, and what does it do to its drawdowns?
options: Leverage increases the Sharpe ratio and leaves drawdowns unchanged
Leverage leaves the Sharpe ratio unchanged (since return and volatility scale by the same factor) but directly amplifies the dollar magnitude of drawdowns
Leverage decreases both the Sharpe ratio and drawdowns
Leverage has no effect on either
questions.explain: Because leverage scales both expected return and volatility by the same factor, the Sharpe ratio is theoretically unchanged, but the dollar size of any drawdown scales up directly with the leverage ratio, along with margin-call risk.

questions.q: What is the difference between gross exposure and net exposure in a long-short portfolio?
options: They are always equal in any portfolio
Gross exposure is the sum of absolute position sizes (long + short); net exposure is the signed sum (long - short), reflecting market-direction risk
Gross exposure only applies to options; net exposure only applies to stocks
Net exposure is always larger than gross exposure
questions.explain: Gross exposure (e.g., 100% long + 100% short = 200% gross) matters for margin and financing; net exposure (0% in that example) reflects the portfolio's actual sensitivity to overall market direction.

questions.q: Why is leveraging up a Kelly-style sizing estimate described as a realistic way to blow up an otherwise sound strategy?
options: Because leverage is prohibited by every exchange
Because the Kelly estimate is based on a noisy, uncertain mu, and adding borrowed leverage on top compounds that estimation-error risk with real, forced exposure
Because Kelly sizing cannot be combined with leverage under any circumstances
Because leverage always reduces expected returns
questions.explain: If the original Kelly-style estimate overstated the true edge due to sampling error, applying leverage on top scales up a position based on an edge that may not really be as large as estimated — a well-documented way strategies that looked correct on paper produce real losses.
